papers.title: Simultaneous Gradient Learning in First-Price Auctions
papers.abstract: We study equilibrium learning in discretized Bayesian games, focusing on first-price auctions as a testbed for gradient-based learning dynamics under private information. While the symmetric independent private values model admits a unique Bayesian correlated equilibrium (BCE) in the continuous limit, standard convergence guarantees for gradient-based learners do not apply: classical no-regret theory predicts convergence only to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), which can remain large and far from the competitive equilibrium even under fine discretizations. To bridge this gap, we introduce the notion of Bayesian semicoarse correlated equilibrium (BSCCE), an equilibrium concept that refines BCCE by restricting deviations to probability-preserving transformations consistent with projected gradient dynamics. We provide a linear programming characterization of BSCCE with polynomially many variables and constraints and establish the inclusion hierarchy $BCE \subseteq BSCCE \subseteq BCCE$. Our main finding is that the BSCCE set contracts in many cases as the discretization of the Bayesian game is refined. Even with priors for which BCCE fails to concentrate, the diameter of the BSCCE polytope shrinks toward zero, indicating convergence to the unique continuous-game Bayes-Nash equilibrium. These results provide a principled explanation for the observed robustness of gradient-based learning in discretized Bayesian games, showing that these dynamics select a smaller equilibrium set than standard no-regret theory predicts.

papers.title: Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
papers.abstract: Classical theory predicts that irrational traders lose money to rational traders and are eventually driven out of the market. Yet noise trading, herding, and heuristic trading persist even in highly developed markets. We model a financial market as an ecology of two trading-behavior types, relatively rational (R) and boundedly rational (N), whose composition evolves under replicator dynamics according to relative performance. Each type's fitness depends on the share of the other type and on frictions. When the interaction is complementary, that is, rational traders profit from the mispricing created by boundedly rational traders while the latter benefit from the liquidity and price correction supplied by the former, and when the difference in frictions is moderate, a unique interior composition exists and is globally asymptotically stable: bounded rationality persists endogenously. When the interaction is antagonistic, the same point becomes a tipping threshold between two one-type regimes. Comparative statics show that lowering the costs of disciplined trading, as algorithmic and AI-based trading does, shifts the composition toward rational trading continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless the cost advantage exceeds an explicit threshold.

papers.title: Finding Competitive Equilibria in Online Marketplaces with Platform Fees, Taxes, and Subsidies
papers.abstract: We study equilibrium computation in multi-unit trading networks with valuations satisfying generalized full substitutes and agent- and transaction-specific piecewise-linear transfer functions. These transfers model platform fees, taxes, subsidies, and membership discounts in online marketplaces. Our ascending procedure raises prices at different rates and reaches the minimum equilibrium price vector in finitely many iterations, each implementable in strongly polynomial time under our oracle and arithmetic models. An equilibrium allocation can then be recovered efficiently. The method extends primal-dual techniques developed for ascending auctions to handle complementarities between purchases and sales through a submodular flow formulation. In single-seller markets with substitutes and complements, our framework also extends the double-track auctions of Sun and Yang (2009) and Shioura and Yang (2015) to bidder- and good-specific transfers.

papers.title: Asymmetric Rationality: Protocol Design and Behavioral Anomalies
papers.abstract: We study how asymmetric rationality in strategic interactions can generate seemingly anomalous patterns of belief updating and behavior. A boundedly rational receiver designs a finite-state decision protocol to learn from a fully rational, privately informed, and biased sender who controls the flow of information. The receiver must allocate scarce memory between learning and incentive provision. We identify a simple class of protocols sufficient for optimal design and show how their structure generates information disengagement, indecision, and polarization. The receiver hesitates before deciding but becomes unresponsive to further evidence afterward. Identical receivers following the same protocol can reach opposing decisions despite receiving the same sequence of signals, with the probability of disagreement remaining bounded away from zero as their payoffs approach the optimum. These behaviors, which might otherwise appear erratic or psychologically driven, arise from the strategic use of limited memory.

papers.title: The Welfare Limits of Market Segmentation with Captive Consumers
papers.abstract: In a duopoly with captive and contested consumers, I characterize every pair of consumer and producer surplus that can arise under some market composition and some public segmentation, and construct a market that produces each pair. The set is lens-shaped. At any level of industry profit, consumers do worst when captive and contested consumers are perfectly separated and best in an unsegmented market in which the two firms have equally many captives. A market with unequal captive bases and some contested consumers cannot reach this upper frontier under any segmentation. Between Bertrand competition and monopoly, the frontier itself lies strictly below what consumers would get if everyone paid a single deterministic price yielding the same profit. Firms must randomize, and with downward-sloping demand the resulting price dispersion lowers consumer surplus.

papers.title: Calibrated Forecasting and Persuasion
papers.abstract: We study a dynamic game where an expert sends probabilistic forecasts to a decision-maker. The decision-maker verifies these forecasts using a calibration test based on past data. How should the expert send forecasts to maximize her payoff while passing the test? For a stationary ergodic process, we characterize the optimal forecasting strategy by reducing the dynamic game to a static persuasion problem. Calibration restricts long-run forecast distributions to mean-preserving contractions of the distribution of truthful forecasts. We compare the payoffs attainable by an informed and uninformed expert, providing a benchmark for the value of information. Finally, we consider a decision-maker who uses a mean-based learning strategy and show that the expert can guarantee at least the calibration benchmark and sometimes strictly more.

papers.title: Dividing a cake for the irrationally entitled
papers.abstract: A perfectly divisible cake is to be divided among a group of agents. Each agent is entitled to a share between zero and one, and these entitlements are compatible in that they sum to one. The mediator does not know the preferences of the agents, but can query the agents to make cuts and appraise slices in order to learn. For each entitlement profile, we provide a lower bound on the number of queries that the mediator requires to construct an allocation that respects the entitlements regardless of preferences. If one of the entitlements is irrational, then the mediator requires an arbitrarily large number of queries.

papers.title: The Limits of Price Discrimination When the Market Is Unknown
papers.abstract: Bergemann, Brooks, and Morris (2015) characterize the consumer and producer surplus pairs that segmentation can produce when the distribution of values is known. I fix only the set of possible values and characterize the pairs that some market and some segmentation can produce. They form a convex polygon. Its outer edge is the largest efficient surplus a market can have when its uniform-price profit is capped, net of that profit, and truncated equal-revenue markets attain it. At the values no segmentation is needed; strictly between two values, reaching the frontier requires splitting a market into two extremal markets. With a continuum of values up to $\bar{v}$, consumer surplus is at most $\pi\ln(\bar{v}/\pi)$ when producer surplus (the seller's profit) is $\pi$, this bound is reached without segmentation, and no market gives consumers more than $\bar{v}/e$.

papers.title: A Sequential Foundation for Two-Level Nested Logit
papers.abstract: I show that the two-level nested logit demand model arises exactly from a sequential choice process in which group, subgroup, and product taste shocks are revealed stage by stage. The result extends to any number of levels and holds for any nesting parameters below one, without the bounds and ordering that random utility maximization requires. Estimates that applied work discards for violating these bounds are therefore consistent with sequential choice. The standard linear inversion and welfare formula remain valid. Adding a product to a nest can raise another product's share in that nest, even with single-unit demand.

papers.title: How to Pick a Model if You Must
papers.abstract: I axiomatize Berk-Nash equilibrium in decision problems with possibly misspecified models. I specify how a rule--which selects a set of action-belief pairs in a problem--ought to compare a correct forecast with an incorrect one, react to the removal of models, and accommodate additional observations that do not distinguish among the models. Together with axioms concerning attitudes toward randomization and payoffs, and a pair of regularity conditions, these axioms characterize Berk-Nash equilibrium.

papers.title: Optimal Information Disclosure in Classic Auctions Revisited: Endogenous Information Acquisition and Costly Verification
papers.abstract: We revisit the influential distribution-independent optimal disclosure result of Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022), whose optimal disclosure policy reveals low bidder values and pools high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders, and show that this policy is no longer generally revenue-maximizing even for the familiar uniform and binary valuation distributions, once bidders can endogenously acquire private information through costly verification. The underlying reason reflects a fundamental principle of incentive-based mechanism design, rooted in Hurwicz's analysis of structural invariance and echoed in the Lucas critique: economic agents respond strategically to changes in the information and incentives they face. This is the essence of \emph{trust, but verify}. A change in disclosure policy may leave the underlying economic primitives unchanged while altering bidders' verification decisions and the resulting equilibrium information structure. We establish existence and uniqueness of the symmetric Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium, characterize equilibrium-implementable disclosure policies, and derive an exact revenue decomposition and a general characterization of global optimality. We further develop optimality conditions and structural results that provide a systematic foundation for analyzing optimal disclosure with endogenous information acquisition.

papers.title: When an effort-maximizing team architecture is unstable
papers.abstract: Organizations choose team structures to intensify competition, yet their members may prefer to reorganize. We ask whether an architecture that maximizes aggregate effort can remain stable when contestants may form a replacement team from incumbent rosters. When a coalition draws from identical teams and reproduces their type, its members and the designer rank the reorganization in opposite directions: the coalition gains precisely when total effort falls. A strict effort optimum can therefore supply its own blocking certificate, while a stable optimum can survive only on a plateau where every reachable reorganization of this kind leaves effort unchanged. In a linear benchmark, we characterize stability against every feasible one-team reorganization and global effort maximization over every feasible partition. Except under pair capacity, the two regions do not overlap; with pair capacity, they meet only at one boundary. The ordering persists in a matched quadratic benchmark with strictly convex effort cost, and broader one-step deviation rights cannot restore overlap. Among standardized full-cap designs, the unique stable-effort optimum uses the largest feasible roster and sets incentive concentration at its blocking boundary.

papers.title: The existence of anonymous, stationary, monotone social welfare functions satisfying restricted dominance: an answer to an open question in intergenerational equity
papers.abstract: In this note, we consider social welfare functions on infinite utility streams and answer an open question posed in Asheim et al. (2021, Remark 1). There exists a real-valued representation of social welfare preferences that satisfies monotonicity, stationarity, restricted dominance, and strong anonymity, hence also finite anonymity. Our social welfare function satisfies a stronger finite-rank sensitivity condition, Liminf-Restricted Dominance, in the sense of Asheim et al. (2022) and Asheim et al. (2025). Our construction shows that limited discontinuity is not redundant in Asheim et al. (2021, Proposition 2): once that diagonal continuity condition is dropped, even arbitrary-permutation invariance can coexist with stationarity and non-trivial sensitivity.

papers.title: Who Says What: Strategic Communication in Networks
papers.abstract: We study a multiplayer communication coordination game in which privately informed agents communicate through a social network and choose their optimal actions while balancing them against their own bliss points and those of their neighbours. We show that equilibrium actions are convex combinations of the expected bliss points of all players, with weights determined by a degree-discounted Bonacich centrality measure. We also characterize when players report truthfully, over-report, or under-report their private information, and show that the incentive to misreport depends critically on the receiver's position in the network. A striking implication is that even under identical preferences, fully revealing communication may not be realized, and information transmission may remain coarse in a star network while becoming almost fully informative in a complete network. Finally, when biases are endogenously chosen, strategic responses to neighbours' biases are governed by their centralities, and unbiasedness may emerge as a Nash equilibrium.

papers.title: Recognizing Dominance through Local Improvement
papers.abstract: Strategy-proofness is the traditional standard for predictable behavior, yet participants often fail to play dominant strategies. Most existing simplicity concepts attribute these failures to the cost of contingent reasoning, which they lower by comparing the worst case of the dominant strategy with the best case of an alternative. I argue that there is another approach, one that makes more use of the structure of the strategy set, which I formalize as a neighbor relation. Comparing neighboring strategies can reduce the need for contingent reasoning, and, even with a single contingency, it can simplify the search through the strategy set. I introduce a new simplicity criterion: a mechanism is local improvement solvable under a neighbor relation if repeatedly moving to an improving neighbor always reaches a dominant strategy. Strategy-proofness is the criterion under the coarsest relation, and many classical mechanisms satisfy it under finer ones. In extensive-form mechanisms without duplicate dominant strategies, the criterion under one-situation neighbors is strict action-proofness, which is distinct from obvious strategy-proofness. Among local improvement solvable mechanisms that implement the same outcomes, the criterion predicts more dominant-strategy play where the local comparison is salient.

papers.title: From signaling to interviews in random matching markets
papers.abstract: In two-sided labor markets, interviews precede matches. Rising interview volumes in medical residency markets have motivated signaling mechanisms that let applicants express interest in a limited number of partners. We study how signaling reduces interviews in centralized random matching markets with post-interview shocks. We focus on interim stability, which ensures that agents do not regret not interviewing with each other. A matching is almost interim stable if it becomes interim stable after removing a vanishing fraction of agents. We consider markets with $n$ agents in which agents on the short side, long side, or both sides signal their top $d$ preferred partners. An interview occurs whenever at least one party signals the other. When the probability of a nonnegative interview shock is bounded away from zero and $d=\omega(1)$, short-side signaling leads to almost interim stable matchings. Long-side signaling can fail in strongly imbalanced markets when pre-interview scores outweigh interview shocks. In balanced markets without interview shocks, both-side signaling fails to achieve almost interim stability when $d=o(\log n)$. For larger $d \ge \Omega(\log^2 n)$, under the same probability condition, short-side signaling achieves perfect interim stability, while long-side signaling can fail in imbalanced markets. We extend these findings to propose a signaling mechanism for multi-tiered random markets and identify conditions for incentive compatibility. A technical contribution is the analysis of a message-passing algorithm for stable matchings on trees, together with local availability certificates used to study interim stability on general graphs.

papers.title: Monotone comparative statics under dual submodularity, with an application to aggregate deferred acceptance
papers.abstract: We develop monotone comparative statics for constrained quantity choices generated by convex costs satisfying dual submodularity, meaning that their Legendre-Fenchel conjugates are submodular. We introduce the Q-order, an exchange order for possibly set-valued quantity choices, and prove a dual counterpart of Topkis's theorem. A closed proper convex function is exchangeable in the Q-order if and only if its conjugate is submodular. Exchangeability implies Q-monotonicity of rejected quantities under price and capacity changes; when the conjugate has a sublattice domain, the comparative-statics property is also a characterization. We apply the result to two-sided matching with divisible masses and welfare-generated, possibly set-valued choices. An aggregate deferred-acceptance algorithm is well defined; the availability sequence and the least waiting-time multiplier sequences converge; and every proposal limit selected by the theorem yields an aggregate equilibrium matching. The construction covers classical stable nontransferable-utility matching and aggregate random-utility specifications.

papers.title: Reputation and Delegated Public Spending
papers.abstract: This paper studies a repeated funding relationship between a grant administrator and an implementing agency. The agency is either committed to implementation or able to divert the advance. The administrator chooses whether to fund and whether to verify, but cannot commit to future decisions. We construct a stationary equilibrium in which agencies with intermediate reputations are audited. An inspection either reveals diversion and ends funding or leads to continued funding with intermittent auditing. In the latter case, audits sustain implementation without further revealing type, while a strategic agency diverts unaudited advances. Cheaper auditing makes funding worthwhile at lower reputations. For initial beliefs audited under both cost levels, it raises the administrator's value but reduces expected long-run implemented spending: a higher reputation is required to retain funding, and fewer strategic agencies meet that requirement. For beliefs audited under both programs, better detection at unchanged cost instead raises implementation without changing the probability of continued funding. These results show why project delivery alone need not measure the value of improved monitoring.

papers.title: Welfare at Risk: Distributionally Robust Bounds for Policy Evaluation
papers.abstract: This paper develops a framework to study how the welfare effects of policy interventions are distributed across individuals when those effects are not directly observed. We bound the superquantile of individual welfare changes by the superquantile of conditional average welfare changes, which is typically identified, revealing how gains and losses are spread across the population. We also bound the share of the population whose welfare loss from the policy exceeds any given threshold --- a distribution-free counterpart to average cost--benefit analysis, closer to a poverty-rate measure of policy harm than to a mean welfare effect. We further extend both bounds to allow for ambiguity in the analyst's knowledge of the distribution of observable characteristics: a non-robust bound estimated on one population can be systematically overoptimistic when applied to a different target population, while the robust version, with its ambiguity radius chosen commensurate with the shift, restores a valid guarantee. We illustrate the method in generalized Roy models with subjective participation costs, bounding not only the distribution of welfare changes in the overall population but also, in a result new to this literature, the entire distribution of welfare (and of participation costs) among those who select into treatment --- the treatment-on-the-treated distribution, not merely its mean. We connect these results to the multi-outcome IV framework of \cite{Heckman_Urzua_Vytlacil_2006_REStat}, showing our robust bounds are immune to the instrument-sensitivity problem they document

papers.title: Algorithmic Attention and Content Creation on Social Media Platforms
papers.abstract: We study revenue-maximizing attention allocation on an ad-funded social media platform governed by recommendation algorithms. Attention is costly and can be monetized through advertising or allocated to increase creators' exposure, creating a trade-off between monetization and production incentives. In a two-sided model with heterogeneous viewers and creators under private information, the optimal recommendation mix includes content that is ex post suboptimal for some viewers to leverage network externalities. These distortions are targeted: low-ability creators are excluded, while high-ability creators are subsidized through exposure or monetary payments. Two-sided complementarities reshape content variety and quality, with implications for personalization regulation and advertising markets.

papers.title: On dynamic price formation in the course of capital reallocation driven by differential rates of profit: strict conservation of value supports Karl Marx's theory
papers.abstract: We develop a three-sector model in which Marx's aggregate equalities (total price equals total value; total profit equals total surplus value) restrict a sequence of fully realized states during capital reallocation and technical diffusion. Anchoring one sector's profit rate to the contemporaneous average selects a trajectory without modeling pricing intentions. Before innovation, capital inflow lowers the receiving sector's price and excess profitability along calibrated stable paths, without a demand function. Stability is predictable from value and technical data; near a stable equalization, the receiver's profit rate falls even where its price rises. A labor-saving, capital-intensifying innovation creates temporary extra surplus value and revalues committed capital. At constant real wages the final uniform rate rises, as Okishio predicts; when rising wages keep exploitation constant, it falls.

papers.title: Dynamic Mechanism and Information Design in AI-Agent Environments: A General Analytical Framework
papers.abstract: TThis paper develops a general framework for dynamic mechanism and information design in AI-agent principal--agent environments, encompassing optimal contracting and integrating evolving hidden information and hidden action with partial verification, technological authorization, and multi-agent interaction. It nests conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and conditional dynamic information design, while allowing reporting, action, and information-use decisions to interact through a common continuation mechanism. We establish a dynamic revelation principle and a recursive characterization of implementability in which truthful reporting and post-report obedience are jointly determined through continuation incentives. In quasilinear optimal-contracting environments, dynamic envelope and integral-monotonicity methods yield a verification-adjusted dynamic virtual-surplus representation and identify three distinct margins: dynamic information rents, verification rents, and the implementation cost of hidden action. These margins generate a branched hierarchy separating conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and their joint problem. We also study the joint design of monitoring, information use, and incentives: more informative monitoring capacity expands the designer's opportunity set, but full disclosure need not be optimal, and information use can itself alter hidden-action incentives. With multiple agents, correlated information, peer discipline, coupled incentives, joint feasibility, and continuation opportunities create additional strategic interactions. Although motivated by AI-agent environments, the framework applies more broadly to dynamic agency settings with similar economic features.

papers.title: Rewarding Noise: Incentives in Decentralized A/B Testing
papers.abstract: Many firms that run A/B tests struggle with low statistical power, increasing the risk that launch decisions are driven by noise rather than true impact. We argue that in decentralized organizations, low power can reflect misaligned incentives: product teams choose what and how to test on a customer-facing experience to maximize their private reward, while the experience owner sets evaluation rules and launch criteria to optimize the experience. We formalize this interaction via a principal-agent model and show that evaluating tests using raw impact estimates creates a reward to sampling noise. Correctly calibrated posterior-mean evaluation removes this reward and creates a local incentive to reallocate toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. Using data on A/B tests run at Amazon, we document patterns consistent with these model predictions. After an Amazon experience shifted to posterior-mean-based evaluation in 2024, test volume declined while both precision and the dispersion of true impacts increased, more than doubling signal-to-noise ratios. Our results highlight that A/B testing methodologies can shape not only measurement and launch decisions, but which tests are pursued in the first place.

papers.title: The fiscal limits of efficient trade
papers.abstract: Sustaining efficient trade under private information requires external subsidies. Although a designer cannot avoid deficits on average, they can control exposure. We characterize efficient and truthful mechanisms that minimize the worst-case deficit in markets with many buyers and sellers, under interim participation. This problem is dual to maximizing expected trade surplus under correlation ambiguity, with constraints on submarkets with one agent removed. In bilateral trade, the best deficit ceiling is the competitive surplus in a benchmark continuum market, achieved by a "competitive pivot mechanism". In larger markets, optimal mechanisms are characterized in terms of worst-case residual welfare contributions, but solutions exhibit a complex combinatorial structure. We obtain explicit guarantees under natural participation charge restrictions and establish how the best deficit excess decays as market thickens. Our duality characterization is general and extends to many mechanism design environments (public goods, partnership dissolution), and alternative participation constraints.
